description:
Frutiger Aero Yams is a group of 4 from Perth, Western Australia. Equipped with a Mechanical Engineering background, we have experience in the facilitation and fabrication of physical and digital systems - and we're honestly looking to revolutionise the world. Day by day. Piece by piece. 

We hope you enjoy our project, Ember Meridian.
summary:
Ember Atlas is an interactive, web-based platform developed to transform decades of NASA satellite observations into an accessible visual history of Earth's burning activity.

For over two decades, NASA's MODIS and later VIIRS instruments have monitored fires worldwide. However, differences in their spatial resolution and observational coverage make it difficult to compare observations across satellite generations, which potentially obscures long-term trends.

To address that challenge, we developed Ember Meridian to harmonise MODIS and VIIRS observations into a shared spatial and temporal framework, working towards more consistent historical comparisons. Through an interactive 3D globe, geographic exploration and date-based visualisation, users can explore how fire activity changes across regions and over time.

But our ambitions extend beyond visualisation. NASA has made an extraordinary wealth of scientific data publicly available however, accessing that information and understanding it are two very different things. By translating complex datasets into an exploratory medium, we aim to lower the barriers separating scientific knowledge from those who stand to benefit, whether researchers, students, fire-affected communities or curious minds.

Ultimately, we want Ember Meridian to make open data not merely available, but meaningful, helping more people learn from and better understand our changing planet.
details:
Project Development and Functionality

Our development of Ember Meridian centred on two challenges: how could we meaningfully compare fire observations from different generations of satellites, and how could we make this information accessible to people without requiring a technical background?

At the heart of Ember Meridian is an interactive globe, allowing users to explore where and when satellites have detected fire activity. Users can rotate the globe, navigate through selected UTC periods and examine individual countries or regions through the Spatial Explorer. Individual detections can also be inspected, revealing information such as acquisition time, satellite instrument and fire radiative power.

We also developed an Activity Calendar to help users identify when fire detections were recorded, alongside a short tutorial intended to familiarise first-time visitors with the platform.

One of our priorities was ensuring that the experience felt intuitive. Rather than presenting users with extensive tables of satellite measurements, we wanted to create an environment where they could begin with a familiar view of Earth and gradually explore the underlying observations in greater detail.

Data Integration and Harmonisation

Our primary data source is NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which provides active-fire observations collected by MODIS and VIIRS.

Although both instruments monitor active fires, differences in spatial resolution, detection sensitivity and observational coverage mean that their observations cannot simply be treated as equivalent. VIIRS, for instance, can detect smaller fires that MODIS may overlook, making direct comparisons between raw detection counts potentially misleading.

To investigate these differences, we developed a Sensor Laboratory that allows users to compare MODIS and VIIRS observations over the same geographic area and time period.

A background browser worker groups detections into equal-area geographic cells by UTC day. Within the combined view, each cell containing one or more detections is counted once per day, whilst separate counts preserve the contribution of each instrument. This provides a common basis for examining the observations without treating repeated detections within the same cell as separate areas of activity.

Our current dataset includes MODIS and VIIRS observations from 3–10 October 2026, alongside daily summaries for selected historical MODIS dates. Whilst this demonstrates the platform's approach to geographic and temporal exploration, the historical archive remains incomplete.

We recognise that differences in satellite sensitivity and observation coverage continue to affect comparisons, and that a day without loaded observations should not be interpreted as a day without fire activity. Our methodology therefore represents a foundation for more rigorous harmonisation rather than a fully calibrated historical fire record.

Technical Framework and Development

Ember Meridian was developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with the interactive globe rendered through Canvas 2D and Leaflet incorporated for more detailed regional mapping.

To make NASA's extensive FIRMS records practical to explore in a browser, we used Node.js scripts to process MODIS and VIIRS CSV files into compressed geographic tiles and daily summaries. Rather than requiring users to download and process the original datasets themselves, this allows the application to retrieve prepared information as needed.

The web application is hosted on Vercel, with a separate archive API backed by Cloudflare R2 for storing and delivering precomputed historical summaries.

This architecture was developed with performance and accessibility in mind. Handling large quantities of satellite observations directly within a browser can introduce considerable loading times and computational demands, particularly on mobile devices. By processing and compressing the information beforehand, we sought to make the experience more responsive whilst retaining the underlying scientific records.

AI-assisted development tools also supported aspects of coding, debugging, documentation and interface design. These tools helped accelerate implementation and refinement, whilst our team directed the project's scientific objectives, design considerations and broader development decisions.

Creativity and Design Considerations

One of the more interesting challenges we encountered was deciding how to present such an extensive collection of information without overwhelming the user.

We wanted Ember Meridian to feel less like a conventional scientific dashboard and more like an environment that encouraged exploration. The globe provides a familiar starting point, whilst the Spatial Explorer and Activity Calendar allow users to investigate the observations from different perspectives.

We also considered how to communicate scientific uncertainty without making the experience unnecessarily complicated. A satellite detection does not necessarily represent an individual fire, nor does an absence of observations automatically indicate an absence of burning activity.

Similarly, differences between MODIS and VIIRS cannot be resolved simply by displaying their detections together.

These considerations influenced how we structured the data and presented comparisons. Our intention was not to remove the complexity of the underlying science, but to make engaging with it less intimidating.

Benefits and Intended Impact

We developed Ember Meridian with a broad range of potential users in mind.

For researchers, the platform offers another way to investigate geographic and historical patterns in satellite-detected fire activity. For students and educators, it provides a more tangible introduction to Earth observation and the relationship between satellite measurements and environmental phenomena.

For fire-affected communities, it offers an opportunity to explore available historical observations in regions that matter to them. We also hope it encourages curiosity amongst people who may never have considered engaging with scientific datasets before.

Ember Meridian is intended for education and exploratory research rather than operational fire warnings or emergency response.

Looking ahead, we hope to expand the historical archive, improve geographic and temporal coverage, and validate cross-sensor comparisons against independent observation masks. These developments would help strengthen the scientific reliability of the platform and support more meaningful investigations of long-term burning activity.

Throughout development, we have come to appreciate that making scientific data publicly available is only part of what makes it valuable. Equally important is whether people can engage with that information, interpret it and develop their own understanding.

Ultimately, through Ember Meridian, we hope to demonstrate how thoughtful engineering and accessible design can bridge that divide, encouraging more people to explore, question and better understand our changing planet.
